newsitem.title: JAPAN: S'tomo says Hamanaka loss snowballed over 10 years.
newsitem.headline: S'tomo says Hamanaka loss snowballed over 10 years.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp president Kenji Miyahara said on Thursday an in-house probe of dismissed copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka's unauthorised trades revealed that his losses snowballed over 10 years as he tried to erase them with still more off-the-books trading.

Miyahara also blamed an upward revision of the estimated losses, to $2.6 billion from the $1.8 billion figure announced on June 13, on the need to liquidate positions after the June announcement caused copper prices to collapse.

Miyahara also told a news conference the company felt it was necessary to liquidate quickly the positions that had been concealed by Hamanaka, as they were very large in relation to the overall size of the market and involved high-risk derivatives transactions.
He said Sumitomo's internal investigation, undertaken by a team composed mostly of third parties, had learned that:

-- Hamanaka incurred a loss around 1985 in a transaction that violated company rules, and without reporting the loss to the company, amassed further losses through additional off-the-books trades intended to cover that loss;
Management estimated the initial amount at 6.5 billion yen.
-- As the losses grew, Miyahara said, Hamanaka tried to erase them in a single stroke with massive and multiple unauthorised trades.

-- There were also transactions Hamanaka undertook to raise money to conceal his losses, and these increased the total amount of the losses, Miyahara said. He added that Hamanaka conducted as many as 2,000 unauthorised deals in a single year.

Miyahara said doctoring of documents and Hamanaka's use of off-balance-sheet derivatives transactions and his ability to raise money through unauthorised trades to cover his losses were why the company was unable to discover the massive volume of trades over such a long period of time.
He said a 60-strong task force assembled by Sumitomo was currently checking over 2,000 cardboard boxes of documents as it sought to sort out the details of Hamanaka's trades.
He declined to comment on whether Hamanaka had cooperated with the company's investigation.
"What we want to prove most at the moment is that the company was not involved with Hamanaka's unauthorised copper trading," Miyahara said.
He said none of the trade house's copper traders had been allowed to see any of the documents being reviewed by the investigation, in an effort to ensure the probe's integrity.
He also said the company was not yet at a point where it could include damages or compensation from Hamanaka or third parties in its balance sheet.
